questions.prompt: A and B collect ₹1, ₹2, ₹5 and ₹10 coins in the ratios 3:2:2:1 and 4:3:2:1 respectively. Each has the same total number of coins. If A’s coins are worth ₹270, what are B’s coins worth?
hints: Find the value and number of coins in one ratio block.
A’s block contains 8 coins worth ₹27; B’s contains 10 coins worth ₹30.
questions.solution: A has 10 blocks, hence 80 coins. B therefore has 8 blocks, worth 8(4+6+10+10)=₹240. Thus B is correct; ₹213, ₹275 and ₹282 do not satisfy the equal-count condition.
questions.theory: A ratio specifies relative counts, not relative total values. If denominations d_i have counts kr_i, their number is kΣr_i and their total value is kΣd_i r_i. The mean denomination is therefore Σd_i r_i/Σr_i. For two collections with equal counts, total values are in the ratio of these weighted means. The scale factors for the two ratios need not agree: a block of eight coins and a block of ten coins describe different totals. First calculate a block’s count and value, infer the actual number from the known value, and only then scale the second collection. Check that inferred counts are integral whenever individual objects are involved.

similar_questions.prompt: Coins of ₹1 and ₹5 are in ratio 3:1 and worth ₹80. Find their number.
similar_questions.solution: A block has 4 coins worth ₹8. Ten blocks give 40 coins.

similar_questions.prompt: Two equal-size collections of ₹1 and ₹2 coins have ratios 1:1 and 1:3. The first is worth ₹60. Find the second’s value.
similar_questions.solution: The mean values are 3/2 and 7/4. The first has 40 coins, so the second is worth 40·7/4=₹70.

questions.prompt: Increasing a train’s speed by 20% reduces the journey time by 2 hours; decreasing it by 20% increases the time by 3 hours. What is the normal duration?
hints: For fixed distance, time is inversely proportional to speed.
The new times are T/1.2 and T/0.8.
questions.solution: T−T/1.2=T/6=2 gives T=12. The second condition confirms T/0.8−T=T/4=3. Only 12.0 satisfies both; 11.5, 13.2 and 14.0 give time reductions different from 2.
questions.theory: For a journey of fixed length D, the relation D=vT implies that multiplying speed by a positive factor k divides the travel time by k. Percentage changes of speed and time are consequently not equal and opposite. Increasing speed by a fraction r saves Tr/(1+r), whereas decreasing it by r adds Tr/(1−r). The latter change is larger. These formulas require the same distance and a constant effective speed; stops must either be excluded or included consistently. When two conditions are supplied, solve one and use the other as an independent consistency check. Convert percentages to fractions before manipulating the equations, and distinguish a percentage of the original time from an absolute number of hours.

similar_questions.prompt: A 25% speed increase saves 1 hour. Find the original time.
similar_questions.solution: T−T/1.25=T/5=1, so T=5 hours.

similar_questions.prompt: A journey normally takes 8 hours. What happens after a 20% speed decrease?
similar_questions.solution: The new time is 8/0.8=10 hours, an increase of 2 hours.

questions.prompt: A tells the truth 30% of the time and B 40% of the time, independently. What is the minimum probability that they contradict each other?
hints: Contradiction is unavoidable when exactly one statement is true.
Both can lie without contradicting, so use only the two mixed cases for the minimum.
questions.solution: Independence gives P(A true,B false)=0.3·0.6=0.18 and P(A false,B true)=0.7·0.4=0.28. These disjoint events force contradiction, giving minimum 0.46, attained when both liars agree on the same false statement. A counts only one case; B is the both-false probability; D exceeds the attainable minimum.
questions.theory: Represent truth-telling by Bernoulli indicators. With independent truth probabilities p and q, the probability that exactly one person tells the truth is p(1−q)+(1−p)q. If both statements address the same fact, one true and one false statement necessarily conflict. When both lie, their statements may agree or disagree if several false answers are possible. Thus the mixed-case probability gives the minimum contradiction probability, rather than the whole contradiction probability in every setting. For a strictly binary proposition, two false answers agree and equality holds automatically. The independence assumption is essential for multiplying marginal probabilities; without it the joint distribution must be specified or bounded. Keep mutually exclusive cases separate before adding their probabilities.

similar_questions.prompt: Independent witnesses tell the truth with probabilities 0.8 and 0.7. Find minimum contradiction probability.
Two independent witnesses each tell the truth half the time about a binary proposition. Find agreement probability.
similar_questions.solution: Both truthful or both false: 0.5²+0.5²=0.5.

questions.prompt: The standard deviation of x₁,…,xₙ is σ>0. What is the standard deviation of 3x₁+2,…,3xₙ+2?
hints: Subtract the transformed mean from each transformed observation.
Every deviation becomes three times its original value.
questions.solution: The transformed mean is 3x̄+2, so the deviations are 3(x_i−x̄). Variance is multiplied by 9 and its square root by 3. Thus A is correct. B ignores the scale, C incorrectly lets a translation affect spread, and D confuses variance with standard deviation.
questions.theory: For any dataset, the affine transformation y_i=ax_i+b changes its mean to a x̄+b and its variance to a² times the original variance. Standard deviation therefore becomes |a|σ. The formula holds for both population variance, with divisor n, and sample variance, with divisor n−1, as long as the same convention is used before and after transformation. Adding b shifts all observations together and leaves their pairwise distances unchanged. Multiplying by a changes every centered deviation by a; squaring explains the a² in variance. Taking the nonnegative square root explains the absolute value in standard deviation. A common error is carrying the additive constant into the spread or failing to distinguish variance from its square root.

similar_questions.prompt: A variable has standard deviation 4. Find the standard deviation of −2X+7.
A dataset has variance 9. Find the variance and standard deviation after y=5x−1.
similar_questions.solution: Variance becomes 25·9=225 and standard deviation is 15.

questions.prompt: A device requires 4 batteries simultaneously. Each battery supplies 2 days of service. With 6 batteries, what maximum running time is possible through strategic replacement?
hints: Count total battery-days and the consumption per device-day.
Split the batteries into three pairs and rotate the idle pair daily.
questions.solution: The available energy is 6·2=12 battery-days; four battery-days are needed per day, so time cannot exceed 3 days. Divide batteries into pairs P,Q,R and use P,Q on day 1, P,R on day 2, Q,R on day 3. Each battery runs exactly 2 days. Hence B is attainable; A is suboptimal and C,D violate the energy bound.
questions.theory: Resource scheduling problems need both an upper bound and a construction attaining it. If a machine consumes k identical resources at once, and resource i has capacity c_i measured in running time, then total operating time cannot exceed Σc_i/k. Equality is not guaranteed by this conservation calculation alone: each resource can contribute only while installed, and all required positions must be filled. With divisible operating periods and interchangeable batteries, balancing the usage can achieve equality when no individual capacity exceeds the proposed total time. In this question a simple pair rotation provides the required construction. Avoid counting batteries sequentially, since four are consumed simultaneously, and avoid discarding partially used batteries when replacement is allowed.

similar_questions.prompt: Three batteries, each lasting 2 hours, power a device requiring two at once. Find maximum time.
similar_questions.solution: The bound is 6/2=3 hours. Use AB, AC and BC for one hour each.

similar_questions.prompt: A device uses two batteries. Four batteries each last 5 hours. Find maximum time.
similar_questions.solution: Total capacity is 20 battery-hours, giving 10 hours. Use one pair for 5 hours and then the other pair for 5.

questions.prompt: Two distinct two-digit numbers are obtained by reversing each other’s digits. Their difference of squares is always divisible by which number?
hints: Write the numbers as 10a+b and 10b+a.
Factor their difference of squares into their sum and difference.
questions.solution: (10a+b)²−(10b+a)²=9(a−b)·11(a+b)=99(a²−b²), always divisible by 11. For 12 and 21 the difference has magnitude 297, divisible by neither 4, 6 nor 10. Thus only D is guaranteed.
questions.theory: Decimal positional notation makes digit-reversal questions algebraic. A two-digit number with tens digit a and units digit b is 10a+b; its reversal is 10b+a. Their difference is 9(a−b) and their sum is 11(a+b). The identity u²−v²=(u−v)(u+v) then exposes universal divisibility by 99, hence by 9 and 11. A universal claim about divisibility must hold for every admissible pair, so a single counterexample is enough to reject a proposed divisor. Distinctness says a≠b; having both numbers two-digit means neither leading digit is zero. These restrictions do not change the factorization. Do not infer universal divisibility from one conveniently chosen numerical example.

questions.prompt: A loan of ₹150,000 bears compound interest at 10% per annum. It is repaid at the end of year 3. What is the total interest?
hints: Compound the principal once at each year’s end.
Interest is P[(1+r)³−1], not the final balance.
questions.solution: The balance is 150000(1.1)³=199650. Interest is 199650−150000=49650. D is correct; A is the simple-interest result and B,C are neither the compounded interest nor the balance.
questions.theory: With annual compounding and no intervening payments, a principal P grows by the same factor 1+r in each year, giving balance A_n=P(1+r)^n. Interest earned or owed is A_n−P. The recurrence A_{n+1}=(1+r)A_n shows why later interest is charged on accumulated interest as well as on the original principal. Simple interest instead gives Pnr, which is smaller for positive r and more than one period. The compounding period must match the rate period; a nominal annual rate compounded m times yearly uses factor (1+r/m)^{mn}. Payments during the term require updating the outstanding balance at their actual dates. Always check whether the question asks for interest alone or principal plus interest.

similar_questions.prompt: Find compound interest on ₹1000 at 20% annually for 2 years.
similar_questions.solution: The balance is 1000·1.2²=1440, so interest is ₹440.

questions.prompt: The field ABCDE has AB=DE=AE=15 m, AB and DE perpendicular to AE. The inward edges BC and DC each make 30° with the corresponding vertical edge (see source figure). Find the perimeter.
hints: AB and DE have equal lengths, so B and D lie at the same height.
Triangle BCD is isosceles with base BD=15 and base angles 60°.
questions.solution: Since BD=AE=15 and the angles CBD and BDC are 60°, triangle BCD is equilateral. Thus BC=CD=15. The boundary comprises five 15 m sides, totaling 75 m. Only B matches; A,C,D would require a different edge length.
questions.theory: When a polygon includes an inward indentation, its perimeter follows the actual boundary, including both inward edges. It is not the perimeter of its convex hull. Here parallel perpendicular edges of equal length place their lower endpoints on a line parallel to the top edge. Subtracting a 30° angle from a right angle gives the base angles of the inner triangle. Two 60° angles force the third to be 60°, and the triangle is equilateral. More generally, in an isosceles triangle with base b and base angle θ, each equal side is b/(2 cos θ). Read angle labels relative to the line indicated, rather than assuming they refer to the horizontal. Diagram scale is only illustrative.

similar_questions.prompt: A rectangular outline has width 12, vertical sides 10 and an inward equilateral triangular notch replacing its bottom side. Find perimeter.
similar_questions.solution: The boundary is 12+10+10+12+12=56.

similar_questions.prompt: An isosceles triangular notch has base 10 and base angles 45°. Find each sloping side.
similar_questions.solution: The equal side is 10/(2 cos45°)=5√2.

questions.prompt: A mother’s age and her daughter’s age are currently in ratio 14:1. In four years the ratio will be 16:3. How old was the mother when the daughter was born?
hints: Let present ages be 14x and x.
Cross-multiply (14x+4)/(x+4)=16/3.
questions.solution: 42x+12=16x+64 gives x=2. Present ages are 28 and 2, so their constant age difference is 26. The mother was 26 at birth. B is her current age; C,D do not satisfy the age equations.
questions.theory: Age ratios change as time passes, but age differences remain constant when both people age at the same rate. A current ratio m:n lets us write the ages mx and nx using one positive scale x. After t years, the ratio becomes (mx+t)/(nx+t), rather than retaining m:n. Cross-multiplication gives a linear equation for x, and the age gap is (m−n)x. To find a parent’s age at a child’s birth, subtract the child’s current age from the parent’s current age. Check positivity and verify the future ratio after solving. Do not add time to the ratio numbers directly, because those numbers represent proportional units rather than necessarily years.

similar_questions.prompt: A father and son are now in ratio 4:1. In 5 years it is 3:1. Find their current ages.
similar_questions.solution: (4x+5)/(x+5)=3 gives x=10. Ages are 40 and 10.

similar_questions.prompt: A mother is 36 and daughter 6. When will their age ratio be 3:1?
similar_questions.solution: (36+t)/(6+t)=3 gives 36+t=18+3t, so t=9 years.

questions.prompt: Five identical spheres of radius 1 are stacked with four mutually adjacent spheres in a square base and one touching all four above, as in the source top view. Find the total height.
hints: Use centers: touching unit spheres have center distance 2.
The base square has side 2; its center is √2 from a vertex.
questions.solution: Base centers lie at height 1 and form a square of side 2. The top center lies above the square’s center. Its vertical separation h satisfies h²+(√2)²=2², so h=√2. Include the lower and upper radii: total height 1+√2+1=2+√2. B,C correspond to different base geometry; D incorrectly uses separation 1.
questions.theory: For identical externally tangent spheres of radius r, center-to-center distance is 2r. Packing heights are easiest to compute from center coordinates, with a final radius added at each exposed end. In a square base of four tangent spheres, the centers form a square of side 2r, and its circumradius is √2r. A fifth sphere touching all four has its center on the perpendicular through the square’s center. The Pythagorean theorem in a vertical plane gives center elevation √((2r)²−(√2r)²)=√2r. Overall height is therefore (2+√2)r. A triangular base yields another formula, so count the base spheres and use the actual diagram rather than recalling a tetrahedral packing height.

similar_questions.prompt: Repeat the square-base stack with radius 3. Find its height.
similar_questions.solution: All lengths scale by 3, so height is 3(2+√2).

similar_questions.prompt: Three unit spheres form an equilateral base and a fourth touches them above. Find height.
similar_questions.solution: The base circumradius is 2/√3. Center elevation is √(4−4/3)=2√(2/3); height is 2+2√(2/3).

questions.prompt: Parties A,B,C,D,E win 30,25,20,10,4 seats and independents win 9. Which statement must be incorrect?

options.B: A and C together can form the government.
options.C: A and D, with all independents, get a majority.
options.D: An MLA from E can become Chief Minister.

hints: Add all seats before setting the majority threshold.
A strict majority of 98 seats needs at least 50.
questions.solution: There are 98 seats, requiring 50 for a majority. A is true because the largest party has 30. A+C=50, so B is possible. A+D+independents=30+10+9=49, so C is false. D is possible if a majority coalition supports the E member; the seat counts do not rule it out.
questions.theory: A strict majority means more than half of the total, so the minimum integer threshold is floor(N/2)+1. Exactly half is insufficient when N is even. Coalition questions require adding seats for the stated groups and comparing with that threshold. A party’s size alone need not determine which member can lead a coalition: a smaller party’s member may be accepted by a coalition with sufficient support. Distinguish a statement that must be false from one that is merely not guaranteed. Numerical data can establish or rule out a coalition’s arithmetic majority, but cannot establish political agreement. In aptitude questions, treat leadership claims as possibilities unless additional rules or commitments are explicitly supplied.

similar_questions.prompt: In a 101-seat assembly, a coalition has 50 seats. Is this a majority?
similar_questions.solution: No. The threshold is floor(101/2)+1=51.

similar_questions.prompt: Parties have 28,24,18 seats in a 70-seat chamber. Can the last two form an arithmetic majority?
similar_questions.solution: Yes. They total 42 and the threshold is 36.

questions.prompt: The source charts give populations in 2010→2020: A 150→160, B 1200→1400, C 180→220; GDP (billion USD): A 115→324, B 1675→2622, C 177→264. Rank countries by the increase in per capita GDP, highest first.
hints: Compute GDP divided by population in each year.
Compare the differences between those ratios, not the changes in GDP alone.
questions.solution: In common units, increases are A:324/160−115/150=151/120≈1.2583; B:2622/1400−1675/1200≈0.4770; C:264/220−177/180=13/60≈0.2167. Hence A>B>C. B and C incorrectly place B first; D puts C first although its increase is smallest.
questions.theory: Per capita output is total output divided by population. Its absolute increase between two dates is G_1/P_1−G_0/P_0, not (G_1−G_0)/(P_1−P_0). Changing denominators can reverse a ranking based on total GDP growth, so both charts are needed. Units common to all countries multiply every per capita figure by the same factor and do not affect the ranking. An absolute increase differs from percentage growth, which is (G_1/P_1)/(G_0/P_0)−1. When a question simply asks for increase, calculate the absolute difference unless a percentage is specified. Read chart labels rather than estimating bar heights and retain sufficient precision when two values are close.

similar_questions.prompt: GDP rises from 200 to 300 while population rises from 100 to 120. Find per capita increase.
similar_questions.solution: It changes from 2 to 2.5, an increase of 0.5 in common units.

similar_questions.prompt: GDP doubles and population rises by 25%. Find percentage growth of per capita GDP.
similar_questions.solution: The per capita factor is 2/1.25=1.6, giving 60% growth.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank so the paragraph’s final sentence is accurate: “THE ABILITY TO REASON ACCURATELY IS VERY IMPORTANT, AS IS THE ABILITY TO COUNT. AS AN EXERCISE IN BOTH, LET US COUNT HOW MANY TIMES THE LETTER ‘E’ OCCURS IN THIS PARAGRAPH. THE CORRECT COUNT IS ___.”
hints: Count the existing E’s, including the quoted letter E.
The inserted number-word itself adds E’s; test consistency.
questions.solution: The fixed paragraph contains 16 E’s. SIXTEEN adds 2, giving 18≠16; SEVENTEEN adds 4, giving 20≠17; EIGHTEEN adds 3, giving 19≠18; NINETEEN adds 3, giving 19=19. Hence only D makes the statement accurate.
questions.theory: Self-referential counting problems are fixed-point problems. First count the occurrences in the fixed part of the text, excluding the blank but including any quoted occurrence of the target letter. If that count is b and a candidate word representing integer n contains e(n) target letters, consistency requires n=b+e(n). Merely counting the original paragraph is insufficient, because completing the sentence changes the object being counted. Test each proposed completion rather than assuming a number close to b is correct. The counted region is the specified paragraph, not the instructions or the option list outside it. Typography such as quotation marks and punctuation contributes no letter occurrences. A tally by words or lines helps prevent accidental omissions.

similar_questions.prompt: A sentence has 5 fixed A’s and is completed with SIX or SEVEN, neither containing A. Which works?
similar_questions.solution: Neither: both give a total of 5 A’s, which agrees with neither 6 nor 7.

similar_questions.prompt: A self-counting text has 15 fixed E’s. Which of SIXTEEN and SEVENTEEN works?
similar_questions.solution: SIXTEEN gives 17 and SEVENTEEN gives 19; neither equals its represented number.

questions.prompt: Datasets A and B have the same mean. Which statement must be true?

options.B: Their means of squared observations are equal.

hints: The pooled mean is weighted by dataset sizes.
If both component means are μ, the weighted mean is μ.
questions.solution: For sizes m,n and common mean μ, pooled mean=(mμ+nμ)/(m+n)=μ, proving D. A fails for A={1},B={1,1}. B fails for A={0,2},B={1,1}, whose squared means are 2 and 1. C fails whenever μ≠0 because it proposes 2μ.
questions.theory: The arithmetic mean of a nonempty finite dataset is its total divided by its number of observations. Combining datasets of sizes m and n gives the weighted mean (mμ_A+nμ_B)/(m+n). Equal component means consequently force the same pooled mean regardless of their sizes. Equal means do not force equal sums unless the sizes agree, and they do not determine spread or higher moments. In particular the second raw moment is the variance plus the square of the mean, so two datasets with equal means may have different mean squares. Universal statements should be tested with small counterexamples. Do not add means as though they were totals, and do not take an unweighted average of unequal-sized datasets unless the component means happen to agree.

questions.prompt: Among 45 people, 40 all know one another and the other 5 know nobody. Acquainted pairs hug; unacquainted pairs shake hands. How many handshakes occur?
hints: Separate pairs involving one outsider from pairs of two outsiders.
There are 40·5 cross pairs and C(5,2) outsider pairs.
questions.solution: Handshakes total 40·5+C(5,2)=200+10=210. C is correct. A double-counts outsider pairs; B omits all cross pairs; D omits the ten pairs among outsiders. Equivalently C(45,2)−C(40,2)=990−780=210.
questions.theory: A handshake is an unordered pair, so N people have at most C(N,2)=N(N−1)/2 pairwise handshakes if each pair meets once. Ordered counting doubles the answer. For an acquainted subgroup of size k and N−k outsiders who know nobody, all cross pairs k(N−k) and all outsider pairs C(N−k,2) are unacquainted. Alternatively subtract the acquainted pairs C(k,2) from all pairs C(N,2). These decompositions are disjoint and exhaustive. The phrase “know one another” identifies a complete acquaintance group, whereas “know no one” includes the other outsiders. Check that every pair belongs to exactly one counted category. Multiplying each outsider’s handshake count without correcting outsider-to-outsider double counting is a common trap.

similar_questions.solution: Only cross-group pairs are unfamiliar: 8·12=96.

questions.prompt: In a group of 7 people, 4 have exactly one sibling and 3 have exactly two siblings. Two people are selected uniformly from the group. What is the probability they are not siblings?
hints: Determine whether the specified siblings must belong to the group.
If every sibling is in the group, count sibling pairs from the sum of within-group degrees.
questions.solution: The source does not state that these siblings are in the group. If all are, the four one-sibling people form two pairs and the three two-sibling people form a triple, yielding 2+3=5 sibling pairs and 1−5/C(7,2)=16/21 (B). But the seven could belong to seven separate families, with all their siblings outside the group, giving probability 1. Hence no option is forced by the literal statement. A is the sibling probability under the extra closure assumption; C,D also do not follow. The conditional intended calculation is supplied without silently adding that assumption.
questions.theory: For uniform selection of two distinct people from N, every unordered pair has probability 1/C(N,2). If the within-group sibling relation forms disjoint full family groups of sizes s_j, the number of sibling pairs is ΣC(s_j,2), so the nonsibling probability is 1−ΣC(s_j,2)/C(N,2). Equivalently, the sum of each person’s number of siblings within the group counts every sibling pair twice. Total siblings in someone’s family need not equal siblings present in the sampled group. A probability calculation must specify the population and the relations within that population. Family sizes alone cannot determine the pair count when membership is incomplete; an explicit closure assumption or a list of within-group family memberships is required.

similar_questions.prompt: A group consists of complete sibling families of sizes 2,2,3. Find nonsibling probability.
similar_questions.solution: There are 1+1+3=5 sibling pairs out of 21, so probability is 16/21.

similar_questions.prompt: A sample contains one person from each of five different families. Each has two siblings outside the sample. Find nonsibling probability.
similar_questions.solution: All C(5,2)=10 sampled pairs are nonsiblings, so probability is 1.

questions.source_note: Literal source does not say siblings are within the group. Option B follows only after adding that membership assumption.

questions.prompt: Two points on a spherical globe of radius 10 have distance 25 units. Under uniform expansion to radius 50, what is their distance?
hints: Uniform expansion multiplies every length by the radius ratio.
The scale factor is 50/10=5.
questions.solution: The surface distance becomes 5·25=125, so B is correct. A,C use wrong linear factors; D uses the area factor 25. The initial 25 exceeds diameter 20, so the stated distance must be along the globe’s surface, consistent with arc length rθ.
questions.theory: A uniform geometric dilation with factor k multiplies every length by k, every area by k² and every volume by k³. On a sphere, an arc subtending a fixed central angle θ has length rθ, so expanding the radius preserves θ and scales arc length linearly. Chord lengths also scale linearly, although the distance in this source cannot be a chord because it exceeds the original diameter. The question’s common units are retained; there is no unit-conversion factor. Distinguish the dimension of the requested quantity before using a scaling law. A radius change from r to R gives length factor R/r, not an additive change R−r or a squared factor appropriate to surface area.

similar_questions.prompt: A globe’s radius doubles. How do its surface area and volume change?

questions.prompt: Which source diagram correctly relates INSECTS, BIRDS, EXTINCT ANIMALS and PEACOCKS? The source provides diagrams A–D.

options.A: Diagram A: one nested pair, a third set overlapping the outer set, and a fourth isolated set.
options.B: Diagram B: one isolated nested pair and a separate overlapping pair.
options.C: Diagram C: peacocks inside birds; extinct animals overlap birds and insects; birds and insects are disjoint.
options.D: Diagram D: two overlapping outer sets, each containing an overlapping inner set.

hints: Peacocks are a subset of birds, while birds and insects are disjoint.
Extinct animals include members of both birds and insects; peacocks belong outside the extinct part.
questions.solution: Diagram C can label its left large set birds, inner set peacocks, middle overlapping set extinct animals, and right set insects. It displays the required subset and intersections. A leaves one category isolated from extinct animals; B has no set overlapping both birds and insects; D forces extra subset/overlap relations between the unrelated categories. Therefore C is the appropriate source diagram.
questions.theory: Euler diagrams depict subset relationships by containment, disjointness by separation, and shared members by overlapping regions. A category such as extinct animals cuts across biological groups rather than sitting entirely within birds or insects. A specific group such as peacocks sits within birds, whereas insects and birds are separate animal categories. To match an unlabeled diagram, assign the most restrictive relationship first, usually the nested subset, and then check every remaining overlap. A drawing with the right number of circles may still impose a false intersection or omit a required one. The existence of an overlap means at least some common members, not that all members of either set belong to the other. Use the source diagram to identify the option, rather than silently replacing its geometry.

similar_questions.prompt: Describe the sets mammals, dogs and fish.
similar_questions.solution: Dogs lie within mammals; fish are disjoint from mammals and hence from dogs.

similar_questions.prompt: Describe students, athletes and tennis players if every tennis player is an athlete and some students play tennis.
similar_questions.solution: Tennis players lie within athletes, and the students set intersects that subset; students may also include nonathletes.

questions.prompt: A boy can escape through a window of size at least 4 feet. There are 28 windows of sizes 2,3,4,5 feet, with counts proportional to their sizes. How many are usable?
hints: Write counts as 2k,3k,4k,5k.
The total ratio weight is 14; include both size 4 and size 5.
questions.solution: 14k=28 gives k=2. The counts are 4,6,8,10, and the usable number is 8+10=18. D is correct. A is the scale factor, B the usable ratio weight before scaling, and C counts only the 5-foot windows.
questions.theory: When category frequencies are proportional to given positive weights r_i, write them as kr_i and determine k from N=kΣr_i. A threshold condition then selects the categories whose measurements satisfy it, and their count is k times the sum of their weights. “At least” includes the boundary value; thus a threshold of four includes windows of sizes four and five. Proportionality refers to counts here, not to total window area or total width. Objects are indivisible, so the calculated frequencies should be nonnegative integers. Keeping ratio weights and actual counts in separate steps prevents the error of reporting an unscaled weight sum. Check that all category counts add back to the stated total.

similar_questions.solution: k=40/8=5. Only size 4 qualifies, giving 4·5=20.

questions.prompt: A 10-question examination awards +2 for correct, −1 for incorrect and 0 for unattempted answers. Which score is impossible?
hints: Let c,w,u be nonnegative integers summing to 10.
The score is 2c−w; examine the largest scores.
questions.solution: −9 occurs with (c,w,u)=(0,9,1); −7 with (0,7,3); 17 with (9,1,0). For 19, c≤9 implies score≤18, while c=10 forces w=u=0 and score20. Thus D alone is impossible.
questions.theory: Discrete scoring problems impose both a linear equation and integer feasibility. With correct count c, wrong count w and unattempted count u, require c+w+u=N and c,w,u≥0 integers. A score ac−bw is possible only when these constraints have a solution. Bounds such as −bN≤score≤aN are necessary but not sufficient; gaps can occur near the maximum because replacing a correct answer with an unattempted one loses a marks, and replacing it with a wrong one loses a+b. Relative to the all-correct score aN, the deficit is au+(a+b)w. This alternate formulation often proves impossibility quickly. Verify possible choices by explicit counts rather than relying only on interval bounds.

similar_questions.solution: Eight correct, one wrong and one unattempted give16−1=15.

questions.prompt: For aₙ=(−1)^{n+1}(√(n+1)−√n), which statement about Σₙ₌₁∞aₙ is true?
hints: Rationalize the positive magnitude and apply the alternating-series test.
The absolute-value partial sum telescopes to √(N+1)−1.
questions.solution: The magnitude b_n=1/(√(n+1)+√n) decreases to zero, so the alternating series converges. But Σ_{n=1}^N|a_n|=√(N+1)−1→∞. It is conditionally convergent, so both B and C are true; A,D are false. The source is a Part B single-answer question, so its options do not determine one correct label. Selecting C as “more specific” would add a convention not present in the wording.
questions.theory: The alternating-series test states that Σ(−1)^{n+1}b_n converges when b_n≥0 decreases to zero. Its remainder after N terms has magnitude at most b_{N+1}. Absolute convergence means Σ|a_n| is finite, and implies ordinary convergence. Conditional convergence means ordinary convergence together with failure of absolute convergence; it is a subtype of convergence, not a mutually exclusive alternative to it. Radical differences often become easy after rationalization, while their unsigned sums may telescope. To classify a series, test both the signed series and its absolute values. In a single-answer item, the labels “convergent” and “conditionally convergent” can overlap, so mathematical truth must be kept separate from an assumed exam preference for specificity.

similar_questions.prompt: Classify Σ(−1)^n(1/n−1/(n+1)).
similar_questions.solution: The absolute sum telescopes to 1, so the series is absolutely convergent.

questions.prompt: Let x,y∈[0,1], x≠y. Which assertion holds for every ε>0?

options.A: There is N≥1 with |x−y|<2ⁿε for all n≥N.
options.B: There is N≥1 with 2ⁿε<|x−y| for all n≥N.
options.C: There is N≥1 with |x−y|<2⁻ⁿε for all n≥N.
options.D: For every N≥1, |x−y|<2⁻ⁿε for some n≥N.

hints: Set d=|x−y|>0 and compare geometric sequences with d.
2ⁿε tends to infinity, while 2⁻ⁿε tends to zero.
questions.solution: Choose N so 2^Nε>d; monotonicity gives the inequality for all n≥N, proving A. B fails because 2^nε→∞. C fails because 2^{-n}ε→0<d eventually. The same fact supplies an N after which no n satisfies D, so D is false.
questions.theory: The Archimedean property ensures that an unbounded increasing positive sequence eventually exceeds any fixed finite number. In particular, 2^nε→∞ for ε>0 and 2^{-n}ε→0. Quantifier order matters: “there exists N such that for all n≥N” is an eventual statement; “for every N there exists n≥N” is an arbitrarily-late occurrence statement. An inequality against a fixed d>0 cannot hold arbitrarily late for a positive sequence tending to zero if it asks the sequence to exceed d. The assumption x≠y is crucial because it makes d positive. To refute such assertions, use the eventual limit behavior rather than testing only one n or one ε. Monotonicity extends a single bound at N to every later index.

Can 5<100·2⁻ⁿ hold for arbitrarily large n?
similar_questions.solution: No. For n≥5 the right side is at most 100/32<5.

Use continuity at π/2 and at π²/7; check tan is finite at the latter.
questions.solution: The first argument tends to π/2, so exp(cos)→1; A is false. The second tends to π²/7>0, and exp(log u)=u, so B is false. exp(sin)→e<π, proving C. Since π²/7∈(0,π/2), tan is continuous there and D’s sequence converges to exp(tan(π²/7)); D is false.
questions.theory: If u_n→u and f is continuous at u, then f(u_n)→f(u). An oscillating term (−1)^n c/n still tends to zero because its absolute value is c/n. Therefore the alternating sign alone does not prevent convergence. For a convergent sequence, limsup and liminf both equal its limit. Composition requires checking domains and singularities: logarithm needs positive arguments, and tangent fails at π/2+kπ. Here the log argument is eventually positive, and the tangent’s limiting argument lies strictly below its first positive pole. Exponential, sine and cosine are continuous everywhere. Evaluate the inner limit first, then check the outer function’s hypotheses, and finally compare the resulting exact constant with the bound in the option.

questions.prompt: How many real roots does x³+3x−2023 have?
hints: Compute the derivative to control the number of crossings.
A continuous odd-degree polynomial has opposite limiting signs at ±∞.
questions.solution: f′(x)=3x²+3>0 on ℝ, so f is strictly increasing and has at most one real zero. Since f→−∞ at −∞ and f→∞ at ∞, the intermediate value theorem gives at least one zero. Exactly one, B. A contradicts existence; C,D contradict strict monotonicity.
questions.theory: A continuous function taking opposite signs at two points has a zero between them by the intermediate value theorem. Strict monotonicity then makes that zero unique. A differentiable function with positive derivative everywhere on an interval is strictly increasing there by the mean value theorem. Combining these facts is often faster than solving a cubic explicitly. Odd-degree real polynomials with positive leading coefficient tend to opposite infinities at the two ends, but they may have one or three real roots depending on their turning points. Here the derivative has no real zero and is always positive, eliminating multiple crossings. Check strict positivity rather than merely nonnegativity when possible, and distinguish the count of distinct real roots from the algebraic degree.

questions.prompt: Which function is uniformly continuous on (0,1)?
hints: A continuous extension to [0,1] guarantees uniform continuity.
Only one option has a limit at the omitted endpoint zero.
questions.solution: B extends continuously by f(0)=0 and f(1)=e⁻¹; Heine–Cantor gives uniform continuity. A has sequences approaching zero with values ±1. For C use x_n=1/(2πn), y_n=1/((2n+1)π): their gap→0 and values→1,−1. For D use x_n=1/(2n),y_n=1/(2n+1), again values→1,−1. These violate uniform continuity. Only B works.
questions.theory: Uniform continuity requires a single δ>0 for each ε>0 that works for all points in the domain. Ordinary continuity permits δ to depend on the point. Heine–Cantor says every continuous function on a compact metric space is uniformly continuous. Thus a function on (0,1) that extends continuously to [0,1] is uniformly continuous. Conversely, a uniformly continuous real-valued function on (0,1) extends continuously to its completion [0,1], since it takes Cauchy sequences to Cauchy sequences. To disprove uniform continuity, find x_n,y_n with |x_n−y_n|→0 while |f(x_n)−f(y_n)| stays bounded away from zero. Rapid endpoint oscillations with nonvanishing amplitude provide such pairs; damping that tends to zero can remove them.

similar_questions.prompt: Is 1/x uniformly continuous on (0,1)?

questions.prompt: For an integer ℓ≥1, find the dimension over ℝ of polynomials in two variables of total degree at most ℓ.
hints: Use the monomials xⁱyʲ with i+j≤ℓ as a basis.
For exact degree k there are k+1 possible exponent pairs.
questions.solution: Monomials are linearly independent and span the space. Its dimension is Σ_{k=0}^ℓ(k+1)=(ℓ+1)(ℓ+2)/2, giving D. A is the homogeneous degree-ℓ count; B,C omit or miscount allowed monomials. At ℓ=1 the basis {1,x,y} already rules out A,B,C.
questions.theory: The total degree of a monomial x_1^{a_1}⋯x_m^{a_m} is the sum of its nonnegative integer exponents. Distinct monomials are linearly independent as formal polynomials and form a basis of a degree-bounded polynomial space. In two variables, exact degree k allows exponent pairs (0,k),(1,k−1),…,(k,0), giving k+1 basis elements. Summing over k≤ℓ includes the constant and yields C(ℓ+2,2). More generally, the dimension in m variables with total degree at most ℓ is C(ℓ+m,m), by stars and bars with a slack exponent. Do not confuse total degree with separate degree bounds: allowing each exponent up to ℓ would instead give (ℓ+1)^m. Homogeneous polynomials include only one exact degree.

similar_questions.solution: Stars and bars gives C(2+3,3)=10: one constant, three linear and six quadratic monomials.

questions.prompt: Let T:ℝ³→ℝ³ have characteristic polynomial f(X). (a) If T≠0 and 0 is an eigenvalue, writing f(X)=Xg(X) implies g(T)=0. (b) If the zero eigenspace has dimension at least 2, the same factorization implies g(T)=0. Which is true?
hints: Cayley–Hamilton gives T g(T)=0, but cancellation of T may be invalid.
For (b), nullity≥2 forces rank≤1; exploit a rank-one operator’s square.
questions.solution: (a) is false: the nilpotent Jordan block T=[[0,1,0],[0,0,1],[0,0,0]] has f=X³ and g(T)=T²≠0. For (b), rank≤1. If T=0, g(T)=0. Otherwise write T=uvᵀ and λ=vᵀu=tr T; then T²=λT and f=X²(X−λ), so g(T)=T²−λT=0. Thus D is correct; A,C wrongly accept (a), and B wrongly rejects (b).
questions.theory: Cayley–Hamilton states that every finite-dimensional linear operator satisfies its characteristic polynomial. From f(X)=Xg(X) one obtains T g(T)=0, but cannot cancel a singular T. The minimal polynomial, rather than arbitrary factors of the characteristic polynomial, determines annihilating polynomials. Rank–nullity gives rank T+dim ker T=3. A rank-one operator has form T(v)=φ(v)u; applying it twice gives T²=φ(u)T, with φ(u)=tr T. Its characteristic polynomial in dimension three is X²(X−tr T), so dividing by one X still leaves an annihilator. Jordan blocks provide counterexamples when the zero eigenvalue has small geometric multiplicity and larger algebraic multiplicity. Distinguish those two multiplicities before removing any factor.

similar_questions.prompt: For a 2×2 nilpotent Jordan block N, does characteristic polynomial X² divided by X annihilate N?
similar_questions.solution: No. The quotient is X, and N≠0 though N²=0.

similar_questions.prompt: Let T=uvᵀ on ℝ⁴. Find a polynomial of degree≤2 annihilating T.
similar_questions.solution: T²=(vᵀu)T, so X²−(vᵀu)X annihilates T.

questions.prompt: For a real 3×3 matrix A, which assertion is false?

options.B: If det A=0, then 0 is an eigenvalue.
options.C: If det A<0 and 3 is an eigenvalue, all three eigenvalues are real.
options.D: If det A>0 and 3 is an eigenvalue, all three eigenvalues are real.

hints: Nonreal eigenvalues of a real matrix occur in conjugate pairs.
Their product is positive, so combine it with the specified eigenvalue 3.
questions.solution: A is true since a real cubic has a real root. B is true by singularity. If the remaining pair were a±ib, its product a²+b²>0; multiplied by 3 it would make det A positive. Thus det A<0 forces the remaining roots real, proving C. D fails for A=diag(3,[[0,−1],[1,0]]), whose eigenvalues are 3,i,−i and determinant3>0.
questions.theory: A real matrix has a characteristic polynomial with real coefficients, hence its nonreal roots appear in complex conjugate pairs. An odd-degree real polynomial has at least one real root by continuity and its opposite end behavior. The determinant is the product of all eigenvalues counted with algebraic multiplicity, and zero determinant is equivalent to zero being an eigenvalue. A nonreal pair a±ib has positive product a²+b², so the sign of the determinant can restrict the remaining roots when one real eigenvalue is known. Positive determinant alone does not guarantee a real spectrum or diagonalizability. A rotation block is a useful counterexample because its eigenvalues are purely imaginary and its determinant is positive.

similar_questions.prompt: A real 3×3 matrix has eigenvalue −2 and positive determinant. Must the other two eigenvalues be real?
similar_questions.solution: Yes. A nonreal conjugate pair has positive product, which with −2 would give negative determinant.

questions.prompt: A real 3×3 matrix A has characteristic polynomial divisible by T². Which statement must hold?
hints: The remaining factor of the characteristic polynomial is linear over ℝ.

questions.solution: The monic cubic is T²(T−a) with a∈ℝ, so all eigenvalues 0,0,a are real: B. A can fail for J₂(0)⊕[1], whose zero eigenspace has dimension1. That example is not diagonalizable, refuting D. C fails for diag(0,0,1), whose cube is itself and is nonzero.
questions.theory: The characteristic polynomial of a real n×n matrix is monic of degree n with real coefficients. A specified factor removes its algebraic multiplicity from the remaining degree. In dimension three, divisibility by T² leaves a real linear factor, so no nonreal conjugate pair can remain. The eigenspace dimension, called geometric multiplicity, lies between one and the eigenvalue’s algebraic multiplicity; equality is not automatic. Diagonalizability requires enough independent eigenvectors across all eigenvalues, equivalently a minimal polynomial with distinct linear factors over the field. Nilpotence requires all eigenvalues zero, so two zero eigenvalues alone do not imply A³=0. Small diagonal and Jordan-block examples separate these claims efficiently.

questions.prompt: For x,y∈ℝⁿ with n≥2, which formula defines an inner product?
hints: Check bilinearity, symmetry and strict positivity on nonzero vectors.
A diagonal weighted dot product works when every weight is positive.
questions.solution: C is bilinear and symmetric, and ⟨x,x⟩=Σj³x_j²>0 for x≠0. A equals (Σx_i)(Σy_j), giving zero norm to e₁−e₂. B is not linear and ⟨x,0⟩≠0 for nonzero x. D gives ⟨e₁,e₁⟩=0 since n≥2. Hence only C satisfies all axioms.
questions.theory: A real inner product is a bilinear symmetric map B(x,y) such that B(x,x)>0 for every nonzero x. Bilinearity forces B(x,0)=0 and scaling in either argument. Matrix forms B(x,y)=xᵀMy are inner products exactly when M is symmetric positive definite. A diagonal matrix with positive diagonal entries gives a weighted Euclidean product. Positive semidefiniteness is insufficient: a nonzero vector with B(x,x)=0 violates definiteness. Reversing coordinates produces a symmetric bilinear form but does not ensure positivity. To reject a candidate, test simple basis vectors, their sums and differences, or set one argument to zero. Verify all axioms before accepting a formula merely because it resembles a dot product.

questions.prompt: For B=[[1,1,0],[1,1,0],[0,0,−2]], let Q(x,y,z)=(x,y,z)B(x,y,z)ᵀ and S={Q=0}. Which statement is false?

questions.theory: A quadratic form on ℝⁿ is Q(v)=vᵀBv, with B taken symmetric. It is degenerate when B is singular, meaning the associated bilinear form has a nonzero radical vector. Diagonalization or direct completion of squares reveals its geometry. A difference of two squares factors into two linear forms; the zero set is then the union of their hyperplanes. Coordinate-plane intersections are found by setting the missing coordinate to zero, not by projecting the entire surface. For this form the eigenvalues are 2,0,−2, so it is indefinite and degenerate. A zero level of an indefinite homogeneous form may consist of lines or planes rather than a bounded ellipse. Keep the form’s algebraic degeneracy separate from individual cross-section descriptions.

questions.prompt: For f(z)=exp(z+1/z), z≠0, find its residue at zero.
hints: The residue is the coefficient of z⁻¹ in eᶻe¹/ᶻ.

questions.solution: Expanding gives Σ_{j,k≥0}z^{j−k}/(j!k!). The z⁻¹ terms require k=j+1, hence residue Σ_{j≥0}1/[j!(j+1)!], C. A,B omit a factorial and D has the wrong exponent relation. For comparison A=B=e−1, while C≈1.5906 and D≈1.5083, so the alternatives are distinct.
questions.theory: The residue of a function at an isolated singularity is the coefficient a_{−1} in its Laurent expansion. This definition applies to essential singularities as well as poles. The exponential series converges absolutely and locally uniformly, and on any compact annulus away from zero the series for e^z and e^{1/z} can be multiplied termwise. Extracting a given power means imposing an integer relation between their exponents. For e^{az+b/z}, the residue is Σ_{j≥0}a^j b^{j+1}/[j!(j+1)!]. Pole limit formulas require a finite pole order and cannot be used at an essential singularity such as e^{1/z}. Write down the exponent equation before matching indices to avoid dropping one of the factorials.

questions.prompt: An entire function satisfies |f(z)|≤eʸ for every z=x+iy. Which conclusion holds?
hints: Multiply f by an entire exponential to cancel the bound.
|eⁱᶻ|=e⁻ʸ, so f(z)eⁱᶻ is bounded by1.
questions.solution: g(z)=f(z)e^{iz} is entire and |g|≤1. Liouville implies g=c with |c|≤1, so f=c e^{−iz}, A. B fails for f=e^{−iz}. C,D would require f(0)=1, whereas f=0 or f=(1/2)e^{−iz} satisfy the hypothesis and have different values at0.
questions.theory: Liouville’s theorem states that a bounded entire function is constant. Bounds involving exponential factors can often be normalized by multiplying by a zero-free entire exponential. For z=x+iy, |e^{iz}|=e^{−y} and |e^{−iz}|=e^y; this sign check determines the correct multiplier. Once normalization gives a bound of one, Liouville yields a constant whose modulus is at most one, and undoing the multiplier characterizes every possible f. A coefficient outside an exponential is not interchangeable with a coefficient in its exponent. In particular exponentials never vanish and equal one at zero, whereas the hypothesis allows the zero function and arbitrary smaller constant multiples. Verify both necessity and sufficiency of the resulting family.

similar_questions.solution: f(z)e^{−z} is bounded by1, so f(z)=c e^z, |c|≤1.

questions.prompt: For f(z)=1/(1−z−z²), defined where its denominator is nonzero, which statement is true?

options.B: f has a simple pole at zero.

hints: Multiply the proposed power series by 1−z−z².
Match the constant, linear and all higher coefficients with1.
questions.solution: (1−z−z²)Σa_nz^n=1 gives a₀=1, a₁−a₀=0 and a_{n+2}−a_{n+1}−a_n=0. Thus D is true and C has a wrong linear coefficient. A is false because denominator roots (−1±√5)/2 are poles; B is false because denominator at0 is1. The expansion holds for |z|<(√5−1)/2.
questions.theory: A rational function is holomorphic wherever its denominator is nonzero. Its Taylor series at an ordinary point has radius of convergence equal to the distance to the nearest uncanceled complex singularity. Multiplying the series by the denominator and equating coefficients produces linear recurrences, explaining why generating functions encode sequences such as Fibonacci numbers. Initial conditions arise from the lowest powers, where terms from some factors are absent. For 1/(1−z−z²), the roots are simple and the numerator never cancels them, so they are simple poles, but zero is an ordinary point. Do not assume a power series represents the function on its entire punctured domain; convergence is local to the disk centered at the expansion point.

questions.prompt: For the counterclockwise circle C:|z|=3, evaluate ∮C dz/[z²(eᶻ−e⁻ᶻ)].

questions.solution: e^z−e^{−z}=0 iff z=kπi; since3<π only z=0 lies inside. e^z−e^{−z}=2z(1+z²/6+O(z⁴)). Thus the integrand=(1/(2z³))(1−z²/6+O(z⁴)) and its residue is−1/12. The integral is2πi(−1/12)=−iπ/6, D. A,B,C have incorrect sign or a factor of2.
questions.theory: The residue theorem evaluates a positively oriented closed-contour integral as 2πi times the sum of enclosed residues, provided the function is meromorphic near the contour and has no singularities on it. Zeros of exponential differences are found algebraically: e^z=e^{−z} is equivalent to e^{2z}=1. Their positions must be compared with the contour radius, since otherwise additional poles can be missed. At a higher-order pole, a short Laurent expansion often beats repeated differentiation. Factor the leading power from the denominator, invert the remaining analytic series using (1+u)^{-1}=1−u+⋯, and retain only terms that can contribute z^{-1}. Counterclockwise orientation supplies the positive 2πi factor.

questions.prompt: Which can be the class equation of a group of order 10?
hints: Singleton conjugacy classes are exactly central elements.
Use Lagrange for the center and the fact that a cyclic quotient by the center forces the group abelian.
questions.solution: A occurs for the cyclic group C₁₀, whose classes are all singletons. B would give center of order2 and G/Z(G) of order5, hence cyclic; that would force G abelian, contradicting the 2-element classes. C gives center order3, which cannot divide10. D has class sizes3,4 not dividing10. Therefore A alone is possible.
questions.theory: The conjugation class of g has size [G:C_G(g)], so each class size divides |G|. Central elements have singleton classes; the sum of singleton terms equals |Z(G)|, which also divides |G|. These necessary divisibility conditions do not always suffice. A useful stronger theorem says that if G/Z(G) is cyclic then G is abelian: write all elements as powers of one representative times central factors, and they commute. Thus a hypothetical center producing a prime-order quotient may contradict nontrivial classes. Every abelian group has only singleton conjugacy classes. When checking a class equation, first verify the total, then class-size divisibility, center order and structural constraints; numerical decompositions alone are not automatically realizable.

similar_questions.solution: No. Its quotient by the center would have order5 and be cyclic, forcing the group abelian.

questions.prompt: How many solutions does x²=1 have in ℤ/105ℤ?
hints: Factor105 into pairwise coprime primes.
Over each odd prime, x²−1=(x−1)(x+1) has exactly two roots.
questions.solution: 105=3·5·7. In each prime field the roots are±1. Chinese remainder gives a unique residue modulo105 for each independent sign triple, so2³=8 roots. D is correct; A ignores±1 and B,C count fewer than the three independent prime factors.
questions.theory: The Chinese remainder theorem identifies ℤ/(mn)ℤ with ℤ/mℤ×ℤ/nℤ when m and n are coprime. A polynomial congruence then holds modulo the product exactly when it holds in every component, and the number of solutions multiplies. In an odd prime field, (x−1)(x+1)=0 implies x=1 or x=−1 because there are no zero divisors and these roots are distinct. Therefore for an odd square-free modulus with k distinct prime factors, x²≡1 has 2^k roots. Composite rings may have additional roots beyond±1 because they have zero divisors. Prime powers, especially powers of two, require their own local counts rather than blindly applying the square-free formula.

questions.prompt: Let p be prime and every g∈G satisfy g^{pⁿ}=1 for some n∈ℕ. Which statement is false?

options.A: If |G|=p⁶, G has a subgroup of index p².
options.B: If |G|=p⁶, G has at least five normal subgroups.
options.C: The center of G can be infinite.
options.D: Some group of order p⁶ has exactly six normal subgroups.

hints: A finite p-group has a normal series with successive factors of order p.
Include both the trivial subgroup and G when counting normal subgroups.
questions.solution: For |G|=p⁶, a central-series induction gives normal subgroups of each order1,p,…,p⁶: seven distinct normal subgroups. This proves B and refutes D. The order-p⁴ member has indexp², proving A. An infinite direct sum of C_p is abelian and every element has order1 orp, so its center is infinite, proving C. Only D is false.
questions.theory: A finite group of order p^n is a p-group. Its class equation shows its center is nontrivial, hence the center contains a subgroup of order p. Quotient by that central subgroup and induct on n; lifting a normal series from the quotient gives normal subgroups of every order p^k, k=0,…,n. There are therefore at least n+1 normal subgroups when the trivial subgroup and the whole group are included. The elementwise p-power-order assumption does not require G to be finite. Infinite abelian examples such as a direct sum of copies of C_p satisfy it and have infinite center. Avoid extending a theorem about finite p-groups’ cardinality to all groups with this torsion property, and make the convention for counting all subgroups explicit.
